principle: Let players skip and pause anything they are not controlling
why: Logos, opening movies, intermissions and cutscenes are moments when nobody is playing. Creators want every sequence seen, but a player with no save data may still have seen it before, and not being able to skip video is flat-out inconvenient. Phone calls, visitors and dinner pull players away mid-scene, and making players wait is, in his words, a sin.
how_to_apply: Let one press skip a whole non-interactive sequence (company logos, opening movie, intermissions, cutscenes, credits), including on a brand-new save. Show a skip prompt the moment any button is pressed during a cutscene. Let players pause in the middle of any cutscene. If you write company or platform logo guidelines, make skippable the default. The only accepted exception for pausing is an online game that keeps advancing.
anti_pattern: Locking the skip until the scene has been watched once; cutscenes that can be skipped but not paused; unskippable logos or credits; cutscenes that ignore button presses.
example: Ep 180 lists logos, opening movies, intermissions and cutscenes as things to make skippable all at once; ep 233 adds the credits; ep 104 asks that any press during a cutscene at least bring up a skip prompt.
review_question: On a fresh save, can a player skip every logo, movie, cutscene and the credits with one press, and pause any cutscene?
keywords: skip cutscene skippable unskippable pause cutscene company logos opening movie credits intermission player time skip prompt

principle: Let players read and advance text at their own speed
why: People read on-screen text and subtitles quickly and zipping through text feels good. Staged, voiced scenes cannot move at the pace a reader wants, like the difference between turning a book's pages and watching a film. Everyone wants to enjoy as much as possible in as little time as they can, as video playback-speed settings show, while others want to slow down, so support both.
how_to_apply: Make one press finish the current text box instantly and the next press advance it. In voiced cutscenes add a skip that jumps to the start of the next line as well as a skip for the whole scene, or a fast-forward. Where possible, deliver dialogue as voiced lines during gameplay so players never stop to wait. Playtest text pacing with fast readers.
anti_pattern: Forcing every player through text or cutscenes at one fixed, slow pace; a text crawl that cannot be completed early.
example: Line-by-line dialogue skip that jumps to the start of the next line, which Sakurai calls a real breeze (211). Kid Icarus: Uprising tells its story during play like a radio program, with an option to turn it off (125).
review_question: Can a fast reader complete each text box with one press, and skip a voiced scene one line at a time?
keywords: text speed advance text dialogue skip line by line fast forward typewriter text crawl voiced dialogue during gameplay reading speed

principle: Ship in-game button remapping in every game, however simple
why: Button settings are a necessity for some players. Modern controllers are not simple and players arrive with diverse mindsets and experiences. Consoles do not offer per-game remapping, and a console-wide remap such as Switch's affects every application and can leave actions with no button. Designers once assumed they had found the best controls so nobody would need to change them; players want the freedom to play how they like.
how_to_apply: Build a key config screen that draws the controller graphically. Let players select a button with the cursor, then pick its action from a list. Allow several buttons to share one action, and let each be reassigned separately. Save layouts under player profile names chosen before a match, stored on the controller where hardware allows. Where actions can go on the directional buttons, confirm a remap with a long press so short presses still navigate. Show each action's default button, split maps by context (aiming, swimming, menus), and make sure no essential action can end up unbound. Keep genre-standard defaults.
anti_pattern: Fixed controls on a modern controller; leaving remapping to the console; press-the-button-to-assign screens that capture the menu's own exit button; vertical lists where players lose track of which button does what.
example: Smash Bros. draws every controller, uses cursor assignment, has two jump buttons and name-based profiles for guest players (197). The Last of Us Part I confirms remaps with a long press and shows the default button beside each action (55). Sakurai remapped Pac-Land's press-A-to-run-right, mash-B-to-run-left scheme to D-pad movement and A to jump (156).
review_question: Can a player rebind every action in-game, save it under their name, and never leave an action without a button?
keywords: button remapping key config rebind controls control settings custom controls profiles input mapping accessibility controller layout

principle: Answer every button press, and accept confirm on several buttons
why: Players press buttons because they want something from the game. Play is a two-way flow from the hands to the computer and back to the eyes and ears, and an action with no reaction feels lacking. Everyone plays their own way; if L also confirms, players can even play one-handed. Feeling around for which button does what is a downside, but it beats unresponsive controls.
how_to_apply: In menus, accept confirm from the main button plus another such as a shoulder button. In games with one or two actions, put each action on several buttons instead of leaving most dead. During cutscenes, respond to any press with a skip prompt. Give every accepted press a clear sound, highlight or animation. For each state (menus, gameplay, cutscenes), list which buttons do nothing and give them a sensible reaction unless silence is deliberate.
anti_pattern: Buttons that produce no reaction; ambiguous feedback that leaves players unsure whether the press registered.
example: Using L as an extra confirm or action button allows one-handed play (104). Smash Bros. has two jump buttons (197).
review_question: In each game state, which buttons currently do nothing, and is that silence deliberate?
keywords: responsiveness unresponsive dead buttons confirm button redundant inputs one-handed play feedback button press reaction menu input

principle: Make the game playable without reading a single word
why: Pictures are recognized much faster than text and parsed largely through intuition, while words must be read and then understood. Many players will not read the on-screen language. Typical interface design sometimes lets mashing confirm reach the game by accident; Sakurai sets it up on purpose because the idea is rarely considered.
how_to_apply: Put a picture or character on every major menu icon. Give each section a color. Set the default cursor on every screen from the title onward so pressing confirm repeatedly starts the main mode, tutorial included if there is one. Switch the game to a language you cannot read and try to navigate it; fix any screen where you get lost.
anti_pattern: Text-only menus that become unusable without the language; default cursors resting on Options or Exit.
example: Mashing confirm in Smash Bros. Ultimate goes from the title to Smash mode's fighter select, in Kirby Air Ride to the first Air Ride stage, and in Kirby Super Star to the first scenario with its tutorial. With menus switched to Korean, the icon pictures still help somewhat (240).
review_question: If every word were in a language you cannot read, could you still reach and start the main mode?
keywords: wordless clarity icons pictures language independent default cursor mash confirm quick start localization nonverbal UI

principle: Size and lay out text for every language and the real screen
why: The right text size varies by language: kanji need larger but fewer characters, English is legible small but runs longer, and French longer still. A layout designed only for English leaves translations too small. Handheld developers who check on the real device quickly spot text that is too small, which is why handheld games tend to use larger fonts. Icon menus are hard to fit in wider languages. Text that is too big stops looking stylish.
how_to_apply: Leave room in every text area for each target language's glyph size and string length. Read every screen, in every language, on the actual target display, including the handheld itself. Mock up labels in your longest language before locking a layout. Keep the interface clean so text has room to grow, and offer a font-size setting where space allows, along with subtitle size options.
anti_pattern: English-only layouts; approving text on a large dev monitor only; text so large it no longer looks stylish.
example: Japanese, English and French text compared (33). Smash Bros. icon menus fit Japanese well but were hard to fit in languages that take more horizontal space (147).
review_question: Has every screen been read, in every language, on the smallest real display the game ships on?
keywords: text size font size localization translation string length readability handheld subtitles legibility typography language layout

principle: Write help text and names in plain words, never the item's name
why: Menu items are usually one or two words that often do not say what they do. Help text exists for people who do not know the term, so describing Options as Go to the Options misses the point, and he says it happens quite often. Being clear in a few words is hard, so you must drill down to the essential meaning. Names follow the same rule: player-facing names should follow how the player experiences the thing.
how_to_apply: Show a one-line description of the highlighted item, for example at the bottom of the screen. Rewrite it without the item's own words: Options becomes Adjust a variety of game settings. Cut excess words, translate meaning rather than words, and reread as someone who does not know the term. Name modes by what the player does (Play Solo, not 1P Mode), drop jargon like config or key repeat, and name moves in input order (Up Special), even if internal labels differ.
anti_pattern: Help text that repeats the item's name; technical terms; internal labels shown to players.
example: Options described as Adjust a variety of game settings; Play Solo versus 1P Mode (229). Players see Up Special because the direction is input first, while the internal label is SpecialHi (22).
review_question: Does any help line reuse its own item's name, or any menu use a term a newcomer would not know?
keywords: help text tooltips menu descriptions microcopy UX writing plain language jargon mode names naming 1P mode

principle: Offer comfort and accessibility options, grouped, previewed and safe
why: Accessibility means design that makes a game more convenient and playable, including for players with disabilities, and players come with diverse needs. Motion sickness comes from on-screen inertia the inner ear never feels. Removing presentation for everyone makes the game less entertaining, so make it optional. Assists that lower difficulty can be switched on by accident, and a player who gives up gets nothing from your challenge.
how_to_apply: Add a dedicated Accessibility menu that also links relevant options from other menus, with presets that switch groups on at once. Put difficulty-lowering options behind an extra unlock step. Include subtitle size, background, speaker names with colors and speaker direction; a screen reader for all text; colorblind and high-contrast modes; a magnifier; footstep head-bob off, locked vehicle frames and a center dot for motion sickness; a blur-strength slider; flick sensitivity; a cutscene-vibration toggle; and difficulty changes at any time without restarting.
anti_pattern: Stripping effects for everyone instead of offering toggles; assists a player can switch on by accident; cutscene vibration that cannot be turned off; difficulty locked at the start.
example: The Last of Us Part I's accessibility suite (55). FPS footstep-shake toggles and locked cockpit frames (129). Blur strength in options (192). Smash Ultimate's adjustable flick sensitivity (154). Changing difficulty mid-game (213).
review_question: Can a player prone to motion sickness, a color-blind player and a player who cannot read small text each set the game up comfortably, without restarting?
keywords: accessibility options settings subtitles screen reader motion sickness head bob colorblind high contrast difficulty assists presets haptics comfort options

principle: Make choosing fast by cutting steps to the most common choices
why: Of all inputs, menu selection is the one Sakurai most wants to be quick. Tapping the analog stick over and over is unsatisfying, while a clicky D-pad feels nice, and tactile feedback makes even selection more immersive. New devices are new opportunities to speed things up. But the more advanced the shortcuts, the less beginners use them, and the UI can lose broad appeal.
how_to_apply: Count the inputs to the most frequent choices and reduce them. Support D-pad navigation with crisp one-step movement and a distinct, clicky feel per step. Add shortcuts as optional accelerators layered over a simple default path. When a platform adds a wheel, touch or gyro, prototype using it to jump through lists, but adopt only uses that fit. In equipment screens, offer a one-press equip-strongest.
anti_pattern: Menus that require repeated stick taps; expert-only shortcut systems as the main way to navigate; shoehorning every function of a new peripheral.
example: Since the GameCube and Melee, Sakurai has suggested a clicky scroll wheel, then called a jog dial, for fast menu selection; it was passed on because wheels are bigger than you would think (169).
review_question: How many inputs does it take to reach the three most-used options from the title screen?
keywords: menu navigation fast selection shortcuts input count D-pad analog stick scroll wheel jog dial clicky tactile menu speed

principle: Size menu elements by how often players use them
why: Size shows which modes take priority, so players reach the most-used options fastest; it is all about ease of access. The GameCube controller follows the same idea with a big A button and small X and Y, so you feel which button to press. Weighting has costs: it loses versatility when all options matter equally, and icon menus are harder to translate.
how_to_apply: Rank options by expected use; make the top ones the largest tiles or icons and shrink rarely used ones. Make a game's dominant action the most prominent. Keep a plain, equal list when options really are equal. Mock icon labels in the longest target language early.
anti_pattern: An equal-weight list when a few options dominate; unequal weighting when everything is used equally.
example: Menus from Meteos onward, including Smash Bros., use icons of varying size; the GameCube controller's big A button (147).
review_question: Does the size of each menu item match how often players actually use it?
keywords: visual hierarchy icon size menu tiles importance priority big buttons layout weighting major minor elements

principle: Settle clarity versus style per game, and organize menus like drawers
why: Clarity and style are arguably contradictory, and clear UI does not always mean good UI, or vice versa. Persona's UI is the most stylish he knows yet hard to parse, but swapping it for traditional menus would lose its appeal. A UI is like a drawer that should be organized sensibly when pulled open. Feature-packed games need drawers on top of drawers, and crafting games leave players drowning in materials.
how_to_apply: Decide early where the UI sits between clarity and style from the game's content and setting. Group related items and plan a window hierarchy proportional to the amount of content. Review each menu for visual guidance, element size, window hierarchy, brightness and saturation, and typeface. Then improve usability wherever it does not break the chosen style.
anti_pattern: Assuming the clearest UI is automatically best; replacing a signature style with generic menus purely for readability; flat menus for huge feature sets.
example: Persona 5's menus; Minecraft players building warehouses as makeshift item folders; Sakurai's own drawers on top of drawers (18).
review_question: Where does this game sit between clarity and style, and does every menu follow that decision?
keywords: clarity vs style menu organization information architecture window hierarchy nested menus UI checklist Persona

principle: Keep the HUD informative without crowding the play area
why: A HUD is useful but can crowd the screen, and every game solves that its own way. Markers that track characters would be an eyesore if always visible. Japanese games tend to show more information and overseas games tend to be more restrained for immersion; Sakurai keeps everything on as a player. On CRTs only about 490 of 525 scanlines were usable, so screen edges were assumed unseen.
how_to_apply: Let tracking elements hide themselves based on distance and situation. Turn HUD panels semi-transparent when a character moves behind them. Keep essential information out of edges a display may crop. Offer HUD size with a preview, and HUD hiding for players who want immersion. Make HUD space earn its place.
anti_pattern: Always-visible markers; HUD elements that cover the characters they overlap; essential information at the very edge of the image.
example: Smash Bros. player cursors auto-hide by distance and situation, and the HUD turns semi-transparent when a fighter overlaps it (254). Kirby's Adventure enlarged the bottom info panel, which limited vertical space and showed each copy ability's picture (11). The CRT safe area (252).
review_question: Does any HUD element cover a character or stay on screen when it gives the player nothing?
keywords: HUD heads-up display clutter auto-hide transparency safe area overscan screen edges minimal HUD immersion

principle: Put navigation information where the player is already looking
why: Sakurai often feels he is just playing on the mini-map while the beautifully rendered world goes unseen. Opening and closing a full-screen map again and again is frustrating. The player sees only a small part of the world, and the more realistic the game, the harder the environment is to read. Consider where players look, and even more, what they will be thinking.
how_to_apply: In playtests, note where eyes go; if they mostly watch the mini-map, move the needed information into the main view. Try a translucent full-screen map players can keep up while moving, with one button for a map-only view. Add in-world guidance such as corner-sharpness markers, shape terrain to lead players, design how a 3D map shows height, and offer optional aids like destination arrows, ledge vibration and audio cues near jump or pickup spots.
anti_pattern: A mini-map so essential it pulls eyes off the world; making players repeatedly open and close a full map.
example: Mystery Dungeon's translucent full-screen map; Forza's visual guidance for corner tightness; Subnautica's vertical map (119). The Last of Us Part I's navigation assistance and traversal audio cues (55).
review_question: During normal play, are players watching the world or the corner map?
keywords: mini-map map design navigation waypoint markers map overlay in-world guidance gaze wayfinding traversal cues

principle: Show loading honestly and in your world's style, never timed to dev builds
why: Nobody likes watching Loading linger, and today's players have little interest in waiting, but a wait is easier to accept when the game shows it is loading. Some presentations hide loading perfectly, like Resident Evil's doors, where an icon would ruin the illusion. Load times usually shrink between development and release, so presentation tied to them breaks. What irritates most is a wait that feels like someone dropped the ball.
how_to_apply: Build one minimal, animated indicator styled after your world that can appear anywhere for any duration, and show it immediately when a load cannot be disguised. Use load-masking transitions only if they still work when final loads are shorter, and never put an icon on top of one. Time every fade and black screen and cut each to the fastest version that still does not feel abrupt; keep a short transition rather than none.
anti_pattern: Silent waits; plain Now Loading text; presentation timed to today's slow dev loads; slow fades into long black screens.
example: The first Resident Evil's door-opening transitions (78, 246).
review_question: When the game loads, does the player instantly see that it is working, in a way that fits the world?
keywords: loading screen loading indicator spinner load times transitions fades wipes black screen waiting Now Loading

principle: Never let color alone carry information players need
why: If a game relies on color alone, color-blind players cannot play it, because certain colors look alike under color blindness. Meteos was the one game of his where color coding really mattered, and he would not call it complete until it was playable for color-blind players.
how_to_apply: Run every color-coded element through a color-blindness filter (Photoshop includes one). Where hues merge, separate them by brightness, without making them so dark they disappear into the background. Back color up with shape, icon or position, and offer colorblind or high-contrast modes.
anti_pattern: Gameplay-critical items told apart only by hue.
example: Meteos blocks checked under a protanopia filter and redesigned with big brightness differences (214). The Last of Us Part I's High Contrast Display (55).
review_question: Under a color-blindness filter, can every gameplay-critical item still be told apart?
keywords: color blindness colorblind mode accessibility protanopia contrast brightness high contrast mode color coding

principle: Color-code menu sections, one dominant color per screen, fit to tone
why: Pictures and color convey more information than words and are understood through intuition, so a color per section tells players where they are. A mishmash of colors on one screen often turns into a mess. Lots of color can make a game feel aimed at younger players, so tone and manner come first.
how_to_apply: Give each top-level menu its own color and theme all its submenus in it. Put large images on panels so players learn options by picture. Keep one dominant color theme per screen; large character art is the exception, since the images become memorable. Set saturation to fit the game's tone and audience.
anti_pattern: Many competing colors on one screen; a bright scheme that overrides the game's tone.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's main menu: Smash and its submenus are red, Spirits and its submenus green. Smash for 3DS/Wii U's character-art panels mixed colors but stayed readable (133).
review_question: Can a player tell which menu section they are in from color alone, with no clash of colors on the screen?
keywords: color coding menu colors section colors palette saturation tone and manner visual navigation

principle: Treat fonts, frames and icons as worldbuilding, but keep them legible
why: Two games with the same essence and content can target different audiences just by changing UI or font, which is much easier than redesigning characters or environments. Fonts and UI are the package the world is wrapped in, and frames, icons, colors and decorations add atmosphere too. Modern taste leans minimalist, but fonts still deserve careful thought.
how_to_apply: Mock up one representative screen in several styles (slick, cute, horror, flashy, digital, regional or historical) and pick the one that fits the world and audience. Budget time for a custom font if nothing fits. Theme backgrounds, frames, icons, loading indicators and wipes, not just the typeface. Check every themed font and frame for legibility at real screen size before locking it.
anti_pattern: Menus and fonts as neutral afterthoughts; default fonts left in place; text styled until it cannot be read.
example: One options screen shown as slick, cute, horror, flashy, digital, Japanese, Victorian, Chinese and South Asian (111). Loading indicators that evoke the world (78); themed wipes such as Smash Ultimate's random victory-screen wipes (246).
review_question: Would a screenshot of the options menu alone tell someone this game's world and audience, and can every word on it still be read?
keywords: fonts typography UI style theming worldbuilding art direction menu frames tone and manner legibility custom font

principle: Show what an option will do before the player commits
why: When customization is part of the fun, the work of customizing must be fun, and it feels like a chore unless players can see what the work will get them. Numbers alone are less intuitive. The right HUD size depends on preference and TV setup, so a preview window is a quality-of-life feature within the quality-of-life features.
how_to_apply: Draw the effect on screen, such as a weapon's attack range, instead of only a stat. Show pros and cons side by side. Give visual settings a live preview, show a dark and a bright reference scene on brightness or HDR screens, and let players change them mid-game to compare. Let players test a build immediately, ideally swapping on the fly. Put a short looping clip beside each new skill's description.
anti_pattern: Differences shown only as numbers; settings whose effect cannot be seen until later.
example: The Last of Us Part I's HUD-size preview and HDR screen (55); drawing attack range on the customization screen (182); short clips beside skill descriptions (85).
review_question: Can a player see the effect of each setting or part before leaving the screen?
keywords: preview settings preview customization screen stat visualization compare equipment options live preview skill video

principle: Make large inventories quick to sort, tell apart and equip
why: Lots of items is good for collecting, but players pile up so much that choosing becomes slow, and look-alike icons make them struggle. Crafting games leave players drowning in materials; Minecraft players build warehouses as their own folders. As a heavy player, a way to sort purchases into folders is the thing Sakurai always wants most.
how_to_apply: Add sorting and categories, make every weapon, part and icon clearly distinct by sight, and include a one-press equip-strongest option, which he calls essential. In libraries or launchers, let players make folders.
anti_pattern: Look-alike icons; unsorted inventories; no automatic equip.
example: Customization screens (182); Minecraft warehouses (18); digital libraries (58).
review_question: With a late-game inventory, how many seconds does it take to find and equip the best item?
keywords: inventory sorting categories folders item icons auto-equip equip best library organization crafting materials

principle: Keep the next goal and the distance to it on screen
why: It is a shame when a game does not keep you thinking about the next reward. Showing current EXP against the amount needed shows how far you have come and how far is left, and the number rising with each enemy keeps you pushing. Sakurai says he wishes he had done more of this in his own games.
how_to_apply: Display current versus required values for the next reward on the main screen and update them on every gain. Consider a checklist where clearing an objective reveals the neighbors' conditions. At several points in a playthrough, ask what the player is working toward right now; if it is unclear, show it.
anti_pattern: Hiding how close the player is to the next reward.
example: Ys (TurboGrafx-16 version) shows current EXP and EXP needed (23). Kirby Air Ride's Checklist reveals adjacent conditions as you clear squares (59).
review_question: At any moment, can the player see what they are working toward and how far they have left?
keywords: progress bar experience to next level goals rewards visibility objective display checklist achievements

principle: Make HUD elements react to play and carry character appeal
why: A HUD should be both easy and fun to use. Fighters are sometimes tiny on screen, so faces turned toward the audience boost their appeal, and moving backgrounds suggest burning spirit where a flat image would not. Meters that change or break with the game state make the HUD informative and fun, and in 3D it is hard to track which opponents you have hit. Even a conventional score feels better counted up point by point.
how_to_apply: Put character portraits in the HUD posed toward the player; animate their backgrounds, for example with upward UV scrolling. Swap meters per ability or mode and visibly break them when a vehicle or character is destroyed. Show icons for hard-to-track facts such as opponents hit or defeated. Animate score gains as a running tally.
anti_pattern: Flat, static HUD art; a score that snaps to its new total.
example: Smash Bros. HUD faces with UV-scrolling backgrounds from Brawl on; Kirby Air Ride's ability meters that break with your machine and icons for opponents you hit; Meteos' alien head that spins faster with the Speeder (254). Counting scores up point by point (200).
review_question: Does the HUD change when the game state changes, and is it fun to look at?
keywords: HUD animation portraits meters reactive UI score counter tally juice feedback character appeal UV scrolling

principle: Present scores and ranks so improvement feels meaningful to most players
why: High scores should feel as good as possible. A unit of measurement changes what the number means (Brain Age, Crash Dollars, Global Smash Power). Raw leaderboard positions tell almost everyone below first that they are losing; landing 400th or 10,000th saps motivation, and nobody wants to hear they are in x-millionth place.
how_to_apply: Choose a unit that fits the fantasy and the direction that suits it (lower is better for an age). Show standing as a number that rises as players improve, measured against the whole player population. Do not show general players the world number one. Consider an elite tier that rewards top players and keeps them matching each other.
anti_pattern: A plain score counter by default; raw position leaderboards for huge player bases.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's Global Smash Power and Elite Smash (170); Brain Age, Wii Fit Age, Burnout's Crash Dollars and Tecmo's Game Deviation Value (200).
review_question: Does the typical player's rank display make them want to play another match?
keywords: score presentation leaderboard ranking GSP rating units motivation inverse ranking percentile elite tier

principle: Use text effects for emotion, and let translators restyle them
why: In text-heavy games, changing how certain letters or words appear conveys emotion and adds flavor, which makes such effects almost essential; one text size feels almost wasteful given comics' techniques. But languages emphasize things differently, so native speakers should decide what reads naturally. Effects may not suit very serious titles.
how_to_apply: Support inline markup for size, color, animation and font on individual words. Store the tags in the localizable script so translators can add, move or remove emphasis without a programmer. Offer several speech-bubble styles and a few clear emotion symbols.
anti_pattern: Effects hardcoded where translators cannot change them; one flat style through an expressive, text-heavy game.
example: Japanese comics' kakimoji and manpu, such as a bead of sweat or a vein mark (93).
review_question: Can a translator change where emphasis falls in a line without asking a programmer?
keywords: text effects rich text markup dialogue emphasis localization translators speech bubbles kakimoji manpu
